cajole

kuh-JOHL · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To cajole is to persuade someone to do something through gentle, sustained flattery or persuasion.

The union rep spent the meeting cajoling reluctant members into voting for the new contract.

Worked Example

It took an hour of cajoling before the toddler finally agreed to try one bite of broccoli.

An hour of gentle persuasion to get one bite of broccoli is exactly cajoling.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

charm: To charm is to make someone like you through warmth and personal appeal, and charm can happen with no goal in mind at all. To cajole is charm with a job to do: gentle, patient pleasantness aimed at a reluctant person until they finally agree to something.

persuade: To persuade is simply to convince someone to do or believe something, by any honest route -- evidence, logic, an earnest appeal. To cajole names one particular route: gentle, flattering persistence that slowly wears down a person's reluctance.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

coerce: force someone through threats or pressure

Where it sits · how much pressure the persuasion applies — encourage → cajole → badger

encourage vs. cajole: To encourage is a mild, generally positive push toward something the person may already half-want; cajole sits higher on the pressure scale, implying real reluctance on the other side that has to be gently worn down.

badger vs. cajole: To badger means nagging someone repeatedly -- more pressure than cajole applies, with none of its charm and flattery.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Cajole comes from French cajoler, of disputed origin -- one theory links it to Latin cavea ('cage'), as if to 'cage' a songbird with sweet sounds, though most dictionaries treat this as unproven.

Use the root in a new word: cage

Use the root in a new word: cage: The disputed cavea ('cage') theory behind cajole is a fun, if unconfirmed, story -- luring someone the way a caged songbird might be lured to sing.
